source.title: an adversarial perspective on unlearning (TMLR 2025)
source.authors: Jakub Lucki; Boyi Wei; Yangsibo Huang; Peter Henderson; Florian Tramèr; Javier Rando

page_placements.theme: Comparing attacks and methods: fine-tuning bounds other attacks; unlearning no more robust than safety training

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study's own evaluations find that several attacks recover targeted capabilities after unlearning, while other attacks fail or recover only part of the capability. This challenges and qualifies claims of robust removal.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own WMDP evaluations and attack results. Cited results from other work and values used only to select attack settings are not recorded. Several logit-lens layer-by-layer results are shown only in figures and are summarized in the paper as ineffective for RMU; exact layer values are not inferred.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own recovery attacks (LoRA fine-tuning, per-layer direction ablation, pruning, enhanced GCG prefixes, perturbations, simple jailbreaks) on RMU- and NPO-unlearned Zephyr-7B-β. It reports WMDP accuracy recovery against near-chance post-unlearning scores, which directly tests A, B, C and E.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude current unlearning (RMU, NPO) obfuscates rather than erases hazardous knowledge. Fine-tuning on unrelated data, direction ablation, pruning and adversarial prefixes recover it, so black-box evaluations are insufficient and unlearning shows no clear advantage over safety training. They add that NPO shows signs of deeper unlearning but at a larger utility cost.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates RMU and its own NPO/DPO implementations using WMDP, then applies a suite of adaptive recovery methods; the recovery recipe is not the original unlearning method. The attacks include LoRA fine-tuning, multi-layer direction ablation, enhanced GCG, and pruning.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with prompt-template use, domain (Bio versus Cyber), direction source and layer subset, and the perturbation threshold. The paper reports that some adversarial prefixes work in one chat-template setting but not the other.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO safety-trained models are recoverable by the same attacks at similar rates (e.g., 57.0 after 10 retain examples, 48.2 Logit Lens).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning methods are no more robust to recovery attacks than refusal safety training.

fits_no_version.finding: Logit Lens shows RMU removes decodable answers from the residual stream across all layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some unlearning methods resist probing-based recovery even when other attacks succeed.

record.problems: The study assumes white-box access and access to the original model for some methods; its evidence is primarily on Zephyr-7B-β and WMDP. Some results are only shown in figures, exact per-model values for the 1000-example retain-set result are not stated in the text, and WMDP-Cyber score gaps are described as smaller and more volatile. The authors also report RMU outputs can be gibberish or incorrect and overconfident under some attacks.
record.rows_left_out: The layer-by-layer Logit Lens curves and detailed fine-tuning sample-count trajectories in Figures 2-9 are not separately extracted because exact values are not stated in the text. The paper's extended perturbation, perplexity, and chat-template analyses in Figures 10-16 are likewise omitted except for explicitly described outcomes and the key threshold result. Table 7-8 direction-source variants and further layer-subset ablations are omitted to stay within 60 rows; principal direction-ablation results and notable setting differences are retained.

untested.parts: Only RMU and NPO on Zephyr-7B-β, WMDP Bio/Cyber; Who's Harry Potter and other unlearning methods are not tested.
Quantization recovery is not tested at all.
In-context information and other-language prompts are tried only qualitatively on RMU (Appendix J.2), with no accuracy numbers.
No robust counter-method is tested; TAR is only mentioned.
Only LoRA fine-tuning; WikiText relearning results are figure-only.

missing.what: Direction ablation without the original model: RMU 52.5/54.6, NPO 49.4/42.2 on Bio; RMU layer-7-only ablation gives 56.7
Chat-template fine-tuning (5 forget): RMU 60.3, NPO 47.6; chat pruning RMU 52.4, NPO 40.1
WikiText fine-tuning recovery curves across 5-1000 samples
Prefilling attack on RMU failed to recover from noise
GCG prefix template dependence: 31.2 without vs 51.4 with chat template
Perturbed prompts transferred to NPO models also raise their accuracy

record.verdict_notes: Record version ids V1-V5 map to A-E. DPO rows are unlinked because DPO is a safety-training comparator. R40 is a non-result. A is also linked to key attack rows so its challenges verdict rests on linked rows. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests WMDP accuracy after RMU, NPO, and DPO and recovery attempts; does not test Who's Harry Potter or other unlearning methods, or establish that all simple attacks fail.
Tests fine-tuning on forget, retain, and WikiText data at several sample counts; does not test every possible small or loosely related relearning set.

Tests layer-wise activation-direction ablation and pruning of selected weights, and analyzes RMU's noise mechanism. Does not test every possible activation direction or establish a general deletion mechanism for other unlearning methods.
Low-bit quantization recovery is not tested.

Tests optimized adversarial prefixes, text perturbations, and some straightforward prompt attacks; does not test recovery through other languages as a successful attack or systematically test in-context information.
TAR is mentioned in discussion, but the study does not test a newer counter-method against the attacks.
